title: Model Serving
shortDefinition: The infrastructure that receives prediction requests and delivers AI model outputs reliably at scale.
definition: Model serving is the production infrastructure that receives incoming prediction requests, passes them to a trained AI model, and returns the model's outputs to the requesting application — the operational layer that makes a trained model accessible and usable at real-world request volumes and latency requirements. A well-trained model that isn't properly served is just a file on disk; model serving is what turns that trained artifact into a reliable, scalable production capability.

sections.title: What model serving infrastructure handles
sections.description: Serving manages queuing, load balancing, auto-scaling, health checks, batching, and monitoring.

content.text: Beyond simply running the model, production model serving infrastructure manages: request queuing and load balancing across model instances to handle traffic spikes without dropped requests, auto-scaling that adds serving capacity during high demand and removes it during low demand to control costs, health checking and automatic failover if individual serving instances fail, batching of multiple simultaneous requests where model architecture allows for throughput efficiency, and monitoring of serving-layer metrics (latency, throughput, error rates) distinct from the model's accuracy metrics.

items: Request queuing and load balancing — handle traffic spikes.
Auto-scaling — add capacity during high demand, remove during low.
Health checking — automatic failover of failing instances.
Batching — improve throughput where architecture allows.
Monitoring — serving-layer metrics (latency, throughput, errors).

content.title: The key insight
content.text: A well-trained model that isn't properly served is just a file on disk — serving is what turns that artifact into a production capability.

Training infrastructure is optimized for throughput over extended periods — processing massive datasets repeatedly over hours or days with large batch sizes on high-memory accelerators. Serving infrastructure is optimized for latency and reliability over many concurrent, short individual requests — it needs to respond to any single request within milliseconds to seconds, handle high concurrent traffic without queueing delays, and maintain high availability rather than tolerating the occasional downtime acceptable during a training run. These are fundamentally different infrastructure requirements that call for different design choices.

content.title: Different jobs, different infrastructure
content.text: Training and serving have fundamentally different requirements — optimize each for its specific job rather than using the same infrastructure for both.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of model serving

content.text: Model serving has limitations. Infrastructure can become a significant recurring cost, especially at high volume. Serving latency can be affected by network conditions and geographic distribution. Auto-scaling may not react quickly enough to sudden traffic spikes. Serving infrastructure requires ongoing maintenance and updates. The serving layer can become a bottleneck if not properly sized, and custom serving infrastructure adds operational overhead compared to managed services.

items: Cost — can be significant at high volume.
Latency — affected by network and geographic factors.
Auto-scaling lag — may not react to sudden spikes.
Maintenance — requires ongoing updates.
Bottleneck risk — can become a point of failure.
Operational overhead — custom serving adds management burden.

content.title: Important
content.text: Model serving is essential for production but requires ongoing attention. Choose managed services where possible and monitor serving metrics continuously.

Building effective model serving infrastructure requires careful architecture, sizing, and monitoring. The following practices can help ensure your serving infrastructure is reliable and cost-effective.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Choose between managed and custom serving based on your needs.
Size infrastructure to actual expected traffic, not worst-case.
Implement auto-scaling to match demand.
Set up health checking and automatic failover.
Monitor serving-layer metrics (latency, throughput, errors).
Consider multi-model serving to share infrastructure efficiently.
Plan for model version updates without serving disruption.
Document serving architecture and dependencies.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure serving uptime and p95/p99 latency — these tell you if your serving infrastructure is meeting production reliability requirements.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about model serving

items.question: What's the difference between model serving and model deployment?
items.answer: They overlap significantly — deployment is the process of making a model available in production; serving specifically refers to the infrastructure handling live prediction requests once deployed.

items.question: Does model serving need to be rebuilt for every new model update?
items.answer: Not necessarily — well-designed serving infrastructure is model-version-aware, supporting rolling updates and rollback without rebuilding the entire serving layer for each model update.

items.question: How does serving infrastructure handle traffic spikes?
items.answer: Through auto-scaling that adds serving capacity during high demand; ClickMasters configures appropriate scaling policies based on your specific traffic patterns and latency requirements.

items.question: Can the same serving infrastructure handle multiple different models?
items.answer: Yes, multi-model serving platforms route requests to the appropriate model based on the request, efficiently sharing infrastructure across multiple models rather than requiring separate infrastructure per model.

items.question: How long does building model serving infrastructure take?
items.answer: 8–28 weeks depending on the number of models and whether you need a single-model deployment or a multi-model enterprise platform.

items.question: Does model serving infrastructure cost change significantly with traffic volume?
items.answer: For auto-scaling cloud infrastructure, yes — serving cost scales with actual usage; ClickMasters models serving cost at your expected production traffic volume as part of the total cost of ownership discussion during scoping.

items.question: What is the difference between online and batch model serving?
items.answer: Online serving responds to individual requests in real-time (milliseconds to seconds). Batch serving processes many requests together, often scheduled, with higher latency acceptable. Online serving is more challenging but necessary for real-time applications.

items.question: What are common model serving platforms?
items.answer: Common platforms include AWS SageMaker, Azure AI, Google Vertex AI, and open-source options like TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe, and KServe. The right choice depends on your infrastructure preferences and requirements.

items.question: How do you handle model versioning in serving infrastructure?
items.answer: Serving infrastructure should support multiple model versions, allowing gradual rollout (canary) and rollback. Versioned endpoints or routing rules enable safe updates without rebuilding the serving layer.

items.question: What is the relationship between model serving and observability?
items.answer: Serving infrastructure provides the data for observability — metrics, logs, and traces from the serving layer are essential for understanding model behavior in production. ClickMasters builds serving observability as part of every serving implementation.
